q-132584.name: Question 1
q-132584.problem: A surface $S$ is defined by $z=f(x,y).$ The curve $C$ is the intersection of $S$ with the plane $y=-3.$ Given that the point $P(1,-3,8)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=\frac{{x}^{2}+1}{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}+y\sqrt{x}$, find the slope of the tangent to $C$ at $P.$
q-132584.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=-3.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P(1,-3,8)$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(1,-3).$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(1,-3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,-3) & =\frac{{1}^{2}+1}{{1}^{2}(-3)^{2}}+(-3)\sqrt{1} \\  & =\frac{2}{9}-3(1) \\  & =-\frac{25}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

q-132581.name: Question 2
q-132581.problem: A surface $S$ is defined by $z=f(x,y).$ The curve $C$ is the intersection of $S$ with the plane $x=2.$ Given that the point $P$ with $y$-coordinate $\frac{\pi }{4}$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=y\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy-\frac{\pi }{3})$, find the slope of the tangent to $C$ at $P.$
q-132581.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point where $y=\frac{\pi }{4}$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(2,\frac{\pi }{4}).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(2,\frac{\pi }{4}):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(2,\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\frac{\pi }{4}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}-\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{8}\end{aligned}
$$

q-64968.name: Question 5
q-64968.problem: A surface $S$ is defined by $z=f(x,y).$ The curve $C$ is the intersection of $S$ with the plane $x=1.$ Given that the point $P$ with $y$-coordinate $0$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=\sqrt{2}x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy+\frac{\pi }{4})$, find the slope of the tangent to $C$ at $P.$
q-64968.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point where $y=0$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(1,0).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(1,0):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,0) & =\sqrt{2}(1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(1\cdot 0+\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

q-132593.name: Question 6
q-132593.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=2.$ Given that the point $P(2,\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
q-132593.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(2,\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(2,\pi /4)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}$ at $(2,\frac{\pi }{4}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(2,\frac{\pi }{4}) & =4\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =4\cdot 1 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(2,\pi /4)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(2,\pi /4)}(y-\frac{\pi }{4}) \\ z-0 & =4(y-\frac{\pi }{4}) \\ z & =4y-\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(2,\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=2 \\ z=4y-\pi \end{aligned}
$$

q-36441.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=0.5.$ Given that the point $P(0.5,2,4)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=y+2y\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)+\frac{1}{x}$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$

The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=0.5.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(0.5,2,4)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(0.5,2)}.$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}$ at $(0.5,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(0.5,2)} & =2+2(2)\operatorname{ln}⁡((0.5)(2))+\frac{1}{0.5} \\  & =2+4\operatorname{ln}⁡1+2 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line: 

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(0.5,2)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(0.5,2)}(y-2) \\ z-4 & =4(y-2) \\ z & =4y-4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(0.5,2,4)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=0.5 \\ z=4y-4\end{aligned}
$$

q-71214.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Given that the point $P(1,\frac{\pi }{2},0)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=2\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)-x\operatorname{cos}⁡y$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
q-71214.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(1,\frac{\pi }{2},0)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,\frac{\pi }{2})}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(1,\frac{\pi }{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,\frac{\pi }{2})} & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(1\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})-1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{2} \\  & =2\cdot 1-1\cdot 0 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(1,\frac{\pi }{2})} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,\frac{\pi }{2})}(x-1) \\ z-0 & =2(x-1) \\ z & =2x-2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,\frac{\pi }{2},0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=\frac{\pi }{2} \\ z=2x-2\end{aligned}
$$

q-71226.name: Question 11
q-71226.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=5.$ Given that the point $P(4,5,-2)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=\frac{\sqrt{{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}}}{2x-y}$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
q-71226.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=5.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(4,5).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(4,5):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(4,5) & =\frac{\sqrt{(5)^{2}-(4)^{2}}}{2(4)-(5)} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{9}}{3} \\  & =\frac{3}{3} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(4,5) & ={f}_{x}(4,5)(x-4) \\ z-(-2) & =1(x-4) \\ z+2 & =x-4 \\ z & =x-6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(4,5,-2)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=5 \\ z=x-6\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $y=5,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=x-6$ (or $x-z-6=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,0,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨1,0,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-i-k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $-i-k$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-(-i-k)=i+k$ is also parallel to it.

q-71221.name: Question 12
q-71221.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=1.$ Given that the point $P(-1,1,-1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=3{e}^{x+y}-\operatorname{ln}⁡|xy|$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
q-71221.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(-1,1).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(-1,1) & =3{e}^{-1+1}-\operatorname{ln}⁡|(-1)\cdot 1| \\  & =3\cdot 1-\operatorname{ln}⁡1 \\  & =3-0 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(-1,1) & ={f}_{x}(-1,1)(x-(-1)) \\ z-(-1) & =3(x+1) \\ z+1 & =3x+3 \\ z & =3x+2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(-1,1,-1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=1 \\ z=3x+2\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $y=1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=3x+2$ (or $3x-z+2=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨3,0,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨3,0,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-i-3\,k \\  & =⟨-1,0,-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve C at P(−1,1,−1) can be given as the intersection of two planes: {y=1z=3x+2

q-71220.name: Question 13
q-71220.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=-2.$ Given that the point $P(-2,-6,1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=\frac{y-x}{\sqrt{x(y+x)}}$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
q-71220.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=-2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(-2,-6).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(-2,-6):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(-2,-6) & =\frac{-6-(-2)}{\sqrt{(-2)(-6+(-2))}} \\  & =\frac{-4}{\sqrt{16}} \\  & =-\frac{4}{4} \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(-2,-6) & ={f}_{y}(-2,-6)(y-(-6)) \\ z-1 & =-1(y+6) \\ z-1 & =-y-6 \\ z & =-y-5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(-2,-6,1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=-2 \\ z=-y-5\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=-2,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=-y-5$ (or $y+z+5=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,1,1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,1,1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-j+k \\  & =⟨0,-1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $⟨0,-1,1⟩.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,-1) & =(1)^{2}(2(1)(-1)-1)=-3\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(1,-1) & ={f}_{y}(1,-1)(y+1) \\ z-2 & =-3(y+1) \\ z-2 & =-3y-3 \\ z & =-3y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,-1,2)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=1 \\ z=-3y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=-3y-1$ (or $-3y-z-1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,-3,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$

Question 14
?

The curve C is the intersection of a surface S, defined by z=f(x,y), with the plane x=1. Given that the point P(1,−1,2) lies on C, and that fy=x2(2xy−1), which of the following gives a tangent vector to C at P?

a
3j+k
b
−j−2k
c
−2j+k
d
2j+3k
e
j−3k
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The curve C is the intersection of the surface with the plane x=1. Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve C at the point P will be given by the partial derivative fy(1,−1).

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative fy(x,y) at (1,−1):

fy(1,−1)=(1)2(2(1)(−1)−1)=−3

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

z−f(1,−1)=fy(1,−1)(y+1)z−2=−3(y+1)z−2=−3y−3z=−3y−1

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve C at P(1,−1,2) can be given as the intersection of two planes: {x=1z=−3y−1

Next, notice that:

  • For the plane x=1, a normal vector to the plane is n1=⟨1,0,0⟩.

  • For the plane z=−3y−1 (or −3y−z−1=0), a normal vector to the plane is n2=⟨0,−3,−1⟩.

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

n1×n2=⟨1,0,0⟩×⟨0,−3,−1⟩=ijk1000−3−1=j−3k

Therefore, a tangent vector to C at P is j−3k.

q-132608.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=0.$ Given that the point $P(\frac{1}{2},0,1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=(y+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)+2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
q-132608.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=0.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(\frac{1}{2},0).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(\frac{1}{2},0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(\frac{1}{2},0) & =(0+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot \frac{1}{2})+2(\frac{1}{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot 0)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi \cdot \frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =0+1 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(\frac{1}{2},0) & ={f}_{x}(\frac{1}{2},0)(x-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =1(x-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =x-\frac{1}{2} \\ z & =x+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(\frac{1}{2},0,1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=0 \\ z=x+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $y=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=x+\frac{1}{2}$ (or $x-z+\frac{1}{2}=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,0,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨1,0,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-i-k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $-i-k$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-(-i-k)=i+k$ is also parallel to it.

Next, notice that:

  • For the plane y=0, a normal vector to the plane is n1=⟨0,1,0⟩.

  • For the plane z=x+12 (or x−z+12=0), a normal vector to the plane is n2=⟨1,0,−1⟩.

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

n1×n2=⟨0,1,0⟩×⟨1,0,−1⟩=ijk01010−1=−i−k
